title: Finite-temperature Quantum Quasinormal Mode Theory for Spatiotemporally-resolved Dissipative Cavity Quantum Magnonics
authors: Lars Meschede, Daniel D. A. Clarke, Ortwin Hess
abstract: Cavity quantum magnonics has ushered in an unprecedented era of hybrid light-matter interfaces in which microwave photons, collective spin excitations, and superconducting or spin qubits can be coupled within a single device architecture, facilitating a versatile platform for quantum information processing. Realizing their full potential, however, requires a theory that can treat non-reciprocal magnetic media, material dissipation and open-cavity radiation losses, as well as finite-temperature fluctuations rigorously and without significant approximation. The dissipative magnonic resonances of such systems are described as quasinormal modes (QNMs), yet a consistent quantization procedure for lossy gyrotropic resonators has remained elusive. In this work, we present a finite-temperature quantum QNM theory, based on macroscopic quantum electrodynamics for non-reciprocal media and complex coordinate transformations, that achieves QNM quantization for a wide class of spatially inhomogeneous, dissipative and dispersive, cavity magnonic systems. We demonstrate the predictive capabilities of our theory via applications to hybrid dielectric-magnonic resonators interacting with both spin and superconducting qubits, evidencing modal interference effects, a continuous transition from coherent to dissipative coupling, spatiotemporal quantum field dynamics, and magnon-mediated qubit synchronization, at both zero and finite temperatures. By addressing the intricacies of modal loss and non-reciprocity in a fully quantum theory of cavity magnonics, our approach enables the quantitative design of hybrid quantum devices that operate under realistic open-system and thermal conditions, without recourse to ad hoc quantization schemes.
summary: This paper introduces a rigorous, finite-temperature quantum theory for cavity quantum magnonics, addressing the long-standing theoretical difficulty of quantizing lossy, non-reciprocal magnetic resonators. By employing macroscopic quantum electrodynamics, the authors provide a unified framework to model complex interactions between magnons, photons, and qubits under realistic open-system and thermal conditions. This enables the quantitative design of advanced hybrid quantum devices.
main_problem: The primary challenge is developing a rigorous, unified quantum theory to describe dissipative cavity quantum magnonics, which must account for non-reciprocal media, material losses, open-cavity radiation, and finite-temperature effects.
main_result: The authors present a finite-temperature quantum QNM theory that successfully quantizes the resonant modes for a wide class of complex, lossy, and dispersive cavity magnonic systems.
method: The theory is built upon macroscopic quantum electrodynamics and utilizes complex coordinate transformations to achieve a systematic quantization procedure for the quasinormal modes (QNMs).
model_or_system: The system involves coupling microwave photons, collective spin excitations (magnons), and superconducting/spin qubits within a single device architecture (cavity magnonics). The theory models the dynamics using principles derived from linearized magnetodielectric resonators.
key_observables: Dissipative magnonic resonances (QNMs), modal interference effects, and magnon-mediated qubit synchronization.
important_parameters: Finite temperature ($T$), non-reciprocity, material dissipation ($\alpha$), and coupling strengths between magnons, photons, and qubits.
main_assumptions: The theory builds upon macroscopic quantum electrodynamics and assumes the applicability of complex coordinate transformations to handle lossy, gyrotropic resonators, moving beyond ad hoc quantization schemes.
paper_structure: The paper likely proceeds by first establishing the physical necessity for the new theory, then detailing the mathematical framework (MQED, complex transformations), demonstrating its application to specific hybrid resonators, and finally showcasing the predicted quantum phenomena at finite temperatures.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant as it provides a systematic, first-principles quantum framework for open, dissipative quantum systems, bridging the gap between classical magnetostatics and full quantum field theory in structured media.
